clinicalPearls: Caused by Australian funnel-web spiders of the genera Atrax and Hadronyche, with the Sydney funnel-web among the most dangerous spiders to humans.
Venom of the male Sydney funnel-web is disproportionately potent, and wandering males in the warmer months account for most severe bites.
The active toxins, the delta-hexatoxins, delay inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels, triggering a storm of autonomic and neuromuscular excitation.
The clinical picture is a combined cholinergic and adrenergic surge — profuse salivation, lacrimation, sweating, piloerection, muscle fasciculation, hypertension and tachycardia.
Life-threatening features include acute pulmonary oedema, severe hypertension followed by hypotension, arrhythmia and raised intracranial pressure.
Primates, including humans, are uniquely sensitive, whereas many other mammals tolerate the venom — a consequence of species-specific channel binding.
Pressure immobilisation bandaging with splinting of the bitten limb is the recommended first aid to slow venom spread.
A specific funnel-web spider antivenom is highly effective and has made deaths rare since its introduction.
reference.pathophysiology: The clinically important components are the delta-hexatoxins (historically termed robustoxin and versutoxin), small peptides that bind voltage-gated sodium channels and slow their inactivation. Affected neuronal membranes remain depolarised and fire repetitively and spontaneously, driving massive release of acetylcholine at somatic and autonomic synapses and of catecholamines from adrenergic nerve terminals and the adrenal medulla. The result is a biphasic syndrome: an early excitatory phase dominated by simultaneous cholinergic and adrenergic overactivity, followed in severe cases by a later phase of autonomic exhaustion with hypotension. Pulmonary oedema reflects a combination of the catecholamine surge and increased pulmonary capillary permeability. Non-primate mammals are relatively resistant because their sodium channels bind the toxin poorly, which explains the striking species selectivity of the venom.
additionalDifferentials: Other spider envenomations, including mouse spider bites that may respond to the same antivenom
Organophosphate or carbamate poisoning with cholinergic crisis
additionalInvestigations: Continuous cardiac monitoring and serial electrocardiography
Chest radiograph to detect pulmonary oedema
redFlags: Fasciculation of the tongue, lips or limbs
Severe hypertension or depressed level of consciousness
reference.prognosis: Untreated systemic envenomation can be rapidly fatal, but with prompt pressure immobilisation, supportive care and antivenom the outlook is excellent and recovery is usually complete; deaths have become very rare since antivenom became available.
pitfalls: Removing the pressure immobilisation bandage before the patient reaches definitive care.
Underestimating how quickly severe envenomation can evolve, sometimes within minutes.
Failing to have antivenom and resuscitation facilities prepared before symptoms escalate.
Dismissing the bite because the spider was misidentified as harmless.
